article.title: What "Wo Xiang Ni" (我想你) Actually Means in English
article.excerpt: 我想你 means "I miss you" only as a complete clause. Of the 31 Tatoeba sentences containing it, 3 are translated "miss", 18 "I think that you…" and 9 "I want you to…" — and three dictionaries have no entry for the phrase at all.
article.metaTitle: Wo Xiang Ni Meaning in English — 想 Is Not Simply "Miss"
article.metaDescription: Wo xiang ni (我想你) means "I miss you" only when the sentence ends there. Of 31 attested Tatoeba sentences, just 3 read "miss" and 18 read "I think that you".

keyTakeaways: 我想你 means "I miss you" only when the clause ends at 你. Of the 31 Tatoeba sentences containing the string, 18 are translated "I think that you…" and 9 "I want you to…".
CC-CEDICT, 漢典 and English Wiktionary all list "miss" as the fourth or fifth sense of 想, behind "think" — and none of the three has any entry for 我想你 itself.
Strip the tone marks and wo xiang ni is also 我像你, "I'm like you": 想 is xiǎng (third tone, U+60F3), 像 is xiàng (fourth tone, U+50CF).
Adding a degree adverb removes the ambiguity entirely — all 12 corpus sentences pairing 很, 非常, 好 or 多麼 with 想你 are translated with "miss".
Across 214 SubhSandesh miss-you pages there were 2,417 views, 11.3 per page, and 43.5% of senders locked the page with a password before sharing it.

faqs.question: Is 我想你 written the same way in Traditional and Simplified Chinese?
faqs.answer: Yes. CC-CEDICT lists all three characters with identical traditional and simplified forms — 我 我, 想 想, 你 你 — so the phrase is unchanged in either script. Their codepoints are U+6211, U+60F3 and U+4F60, all in the CJK Unified Ideographs block charted at unicode.org.

faqs.question: What does 我想你了 mean, and why do people add 了?
faqs.answer: CC-CEDICT gives 了 (le) three jobs: completed-action marker, modal particle indicating a change of state, and modal particle intensifying the preceding clause. On 我想你了 it is the second or third of those, so it reads closer to “I'm missing you now” than to a plain statement.

faqs.question: Can I send 我想你 to a friend or to my parents, or is it only for a partner?
faqs.answer: Nothing in the dictionary entries restricts it by relationship. The real risk is structural, not social: keep the clause ending at 你. In the corpus, 想念 takes objects as ordinary as 大学 (college) and 波士顿 (Boston), so the miss-family verbs are not reserved for romance.

faqs.question: Why does my translation app always give “I miss you”?
faqs.answer: Because it returns the single most probable mapping for the string. Across the 31 attested Tatoeba sentences that contain 我想你, that reading covers 3 of them. The app is not wrong so much as it is answering a different question than the one you asked.

faqs.question: Is 我想念你 more formal than 我想你?
faqs.answer: It is not a formality difference, it is a lexical one. 想念 is a dedicated verb with no “think that” or “want to” reading at all, and English Wiktionary tags it Elementary Mandarin. Using it removes the ambiguity rather than raising the register.

faqs.question: What does 我好想你 mean?
faqs.answer: “I miss you so much.” 好 here is a degree adverb. All 12 corpus sentences pairing 很, 非常, 好 or 多麼 with 想你 are translated with “miss”, with no exceptions in the set.

faqs.question: Does 我向你 mean anything?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. 向 (xiàng, U+5411) is glossed by CC-CEDICT as “towards; to face; to turn towards”, and it needs a verb after it to complete the sentence. It shares the toneless spelling xiang with 想 but is fourth tone, not third.

faqs.question: What is the Unicode codepoint for 想?
faqs.answer: U+60F3. It sits in the CJK Unified Ideographs block, U+4E00 to U+9FFF, whose code chart is published at unicode.org. 像 is U+50CF and 向 is U+5411 — three separate codepoints for what a tone-stripped romanisation flattens into one string.

faqs.question: Is 思念 ever the wrong word to use?
faqs.answer: It is never ungrammatical, but it is marked. Of its nine attested Tatoeba sentences, four use it as a noun rather than a verb, and English Wiktionary's only two citations for it are song lyrics — one from 月亮代表我的心. In a text message it reads the way “long for” reads in English.

faqs.question: Do I need the tone marks when I actually text someone?
faqs.answer: No, because you would send the characters, not the romanisation. 想 and 像 are visually distinct and unambiguous on screen. Tone marks matter only when the phrase is written in pinyin, which is exactly the situation this search comes from.

faqs.question: Is 我想你 what a Cantonese speaker would say?
faqs.answer: Usually not. English Wiktionary gives 掛住 two Cantonese senses, “to think about, to miss” and “to be preoccupied with”, so 我掛住你 is the Cantonese form. The same entry's Mandarin sense of 掛住 is “to get caught (on a thorny object, such as a nail)”, which is not a message you want to send by accident.

article.contentMarkdown:
# What "Wo Xiang Ni" (我想你) Actually Means in English

**Wo xiang ni** is 我想你, and when it stands alone as a complete sentence it means **"I miss you."** When anything follows 你, it almost always stops meaning that. In the Tatoeba corpus, 31 attested Mandarin sentences contain the literal string 我想你. Only 3 are translated with "miss." Eighteen are translated "I think that you…" and nine are "I want you to…". Every one of the three "miss" readings ends the clause at 你; all 28 others continue into a verb phrase.

That distinction is invisible in a toneless romanisation, and it matters if you are about to send it. On SubhSandesh's own "I miss you" pages, recipients tapped the on-screen hug **1,434 times across 138 of 214 pages** — 64.5% of pages got at least one — and **43.5% of senders (93 of 214) password-protected the page** before sharing it, against 38.5% platform-wide. People are careful with this sentence. It deserves to be the sentence they meant.

## Three dictionaries have no entry for 我想你 at all

This is the first thing worth knowing, and no ranking page says it.

CC-CEDICT, the open Chinese-English dictionary published by MDBG, contains 125,115 entries. Twenty-one of them begin with 我, including whole sentences such as 我也是醉了 ("I can't even") and 我的天 ("OMG"). 我想你 is not one of them.

English Wiktionary returns `missingtitle` for 我想你. 漢典 (zdic.net) returns a 404 reading 「route snapshot 不存在」.

That is not an oversight. 我想你 is a sentence assembled by grammar — pronoun, verb, pronoun — not a lexical item, so no dictionary lists it. Which means every gloss you read for it is somebody's inference from the verb in the middle.

## 想 has five senses, and "miss" is the fifth

Here is CC-CEDICT's complete entry for 想 (xiǎng, U+60F3), in the publisher's own order:

1. to think (about)
2. to think of; to devise
3. to think (that); to believe (that)
4. to desire; to want (to)
5. to miss (feel wistful about the absence of)

So "miss" is a listed sense, not an invention — but it is the last of five, behind three flavours of *think* and one of *want*. 漢典's 基本解釋 orders it the same way: 思索 (ponder) → 推測 (infer) → 希望、打算 (hope, plan) → 懷念、惦記 (cherish, keep in mind) → 像 (resemble). English Wiktionary lists eight senses for the Chinese character and puts "to miss (to feel the absence of someone or something)" fifth.

Three independent lexicographic projects, three different editorial teams, and all three bury "miss" behind "think."

## Anything after 你 makes it a different sentence

The 國語辭典 entry served on 漢典 gives 想 a sense 4, 「認為、覺得」 — *to consider, to feel that*. Its illustrative example is 「我想你應該回家一趟。」 — "I think you ought to go home for a bit."

The dictionary's own example sentence for *that* sense opens with the exact string 我想你. It does not mean "I miss you."

The Tatoeba corpus agrees, and quantifies it. Of the 31 sentences containing 我想你: 我想你饿了 → "I think you're hungry." 我想你把真相告诉我 → "I want you to tell me the truth." 我想你快点好 → "I hope you'll get better soon." The only two sentences where 我想你 is the entire clause — 我想你! and 我想你。— are both translated "I miss you," with zero exceptions in either direction.

The rule, then, is structural rather than lexical: **我想你 followed by a full stop is "I miss you." 我想你 followed by anything else is "I think you…" or "I want you to…".**

## Without tone marks, "wo xiang ni" is two different sentences

You typed *wo xiang ni*. Hanyu Pinyin writes it *wǒ xiǎng nǐ*. The diacritic is not decoration.

想 is **xiǎng**, third tone. **像** (U+50CF) and **向** (U+5411) are both **xiàng**, fourth tone — different words. CC-CEDICT glosses 像 as "to resemble; to be like; to look as if."

So 我像你 is also *wo xiang ni* once you strip the tones, and it is a perfectly grammatical sentence meaning **"I'm like you"** or "I look like you." Send that to someone you are missing and you have told them you resemble them.

The two characters are genuinely entangled, not merely homographic in romanisation: 漢典's fifth basic sense of 想 is simply 像, illustrated with Li Bai's line 「雲想衣裳花想容」. A learner reading a tone-stripped transcription has no way to see any of this.

## Three third tones in a row, and what actually happens to the sound

Here is where most pages stop being useful. 我 (wǒ), 想 (xiǎng) and 你 (nǐ) are **all three third tone**. The phrase is not two low tones followed by something else — it is three in a row.

Mandarin does not let that stand. The phenomenon has a name: **third tone sandhi**, a phonological alternation, not a spelling rule. A 2026 study in *PLoS ONE* states it plainly: the Mandarin low tone (T3) alters when followed by another T3, and "the resulting F0 is superficially the same as that of the rising tone (T2)." Its ten pairs of native-speaker participants showed measurable confusion when a task forced sandhi to apply.

Two consequences for you. First, what you say does not match what pinyin writes, because pinyin records the underlying tones, not the surface ones. Second, the exact surface pattern across three syllables depends on how you group them, and reputable sources disagree — so we are not going to print one answer here as though it were settled.

Difficulty here is real and persistent. A 2025 study in *Brain Sciences* recorded Mandarin tone production from beginner, intermediate and advanced L2 learners and found the ranking of hard tone sequences stayed the same at every proficiency level; only accuracy moved. Learning more Chinese does not make the sequence easier, it just makes you better at it.

## 想念 or 思念: which one to actually send

Both are dedicated "miss/long for" words, and English Wiktionary gives them word-for-word identical glosses: "to miss; to think of; to yearn for; to reminisce." CC-CEDICT does not. It orders 想念 as *to miss / to remember with longing / to long to see again*, and 思念 as *to think of / to long for / to miss*. Same instrument family, different lead sense.

| | 我想你 | 想念 (xiǎngniàn) | 思念 (sīniàn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dictionary entry exists | No (0 of 125,115 CC-CEDICT entries) | Yes | Yes |
| CC-CEDICT's first gloss | — | "to miss" | "to think of" |
| Wiktionary level tag | — | Elementary Mandarin | Intermediate Mandarin |
| Tatoeba sentences containing it | 31 | 37 | 9 |
| Typical object in those sentences | a person | a person, a city, a college | the old days, longing itself |
| Safe in a text message | Only as a whole sentence | Yes | Reads like a lyric |

The corpus settles it. 想念 appears in 37 attested sentences with ordinary objects — 我想念你, 我想念大学, 我想念波士顿. 思念 appears in nine, four of which use it as a noun, one of which is about night-blooming jasmine symbolising 思念 in literature. Wiktionary's only two citations for 思念 are song lyrics, one of them from *The Moon Represents My Heart*.

There is a simpler fix than choosing between them. Add a degree adverb. Of the 12 corpus sentences pairing 很, 非常, 好 or 多麼 with 想你, **all 12** are translated with "miss" — 我很想你, 我非常想你, 我好想你. Not one is read as "think." One character removes the entire ambiguity.

## What the pages ranking for this get wrong

We measured this search on Bing's en-US market through an isolated browser on 26 September 2026, because Google returned HTTP 429 on two attempts. Of the nine organic results we actually saw, eight were user-generated Q&A, dictionary scrapers, social posts or an off-topic domain; one was a language-school article.

Bing's AI answer box, identical across two authenticated runs, contains a checkable contradiction. It lists 想 (xiang) = "miss" **or** "think of," then concludes: "Thus, the literal translation is 'I miss you'." Both cannot hold. "Literal" is precisely what the missing-reading is not — it is the fifth sense in CC-CEDICT, fifth in Wiktionary and fourth in 漢典, behind *think* in all three. The answer box also never mentions tone sandhi, despite printing the pinyin.

Our own [guide to saying "I miss you" in different languages](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) has the same gap: it lists 我想你 with a flat gloss and no flag that the reading depends on the clause ending there. This page is the correction.

## If you are the one sending it

When you have the sentence right, the page carrying it matters less than people think — but here is what our own data shows, with its limits stated up front.

Across 214 pages built on the [I miss you page for a girlfriend or partner](/missyou-gf) since 28 July 2026, there were **2,417 recorded views, 11.3 per page on average, and 104 on the single most-opened page**. That figure is page views, not unique visitors — one person reopening a page twenty times is twenty views. The sample is two months and n=214, so no seasonal reading survives it.

Two disclosures matter more here than anywhere. **Nothing in our database is segmented by language or country, so no number on this page is a Chinese figure** — it is a platform-wide figure that happens to be the honest one we have. And the database records **which template was opened, never who received it**, so nothing here tells you anything about recipients. Fields such as city, background music and "together since" are pickers with defaults, and their fill rates are not sender choices.

Be warned about the fit. That template is an **English-language page, and it is built for a girlfriend or partner specifically** — English labels, English prompts, English furniture throughout. If you are a learner writing to a teacher, a friend or your parents, it is the wrong page and we would rather say so. A [one-tap-a-day streak page](/streak) suits the long-distance case better, because the point is showing up daily rather than declaring anything, and it is not recipient-specific. If neither fits, [browse the full template list](/templates) instead. Our own records carry nothing at all about plans or billing, so we are not going to state anything on that either way.

And if 我想你 is what you want to send, send 我很想你. The corpus is unanimous about that one.

Terminology check: the label is third tone sandhi (T3 sandhi), a phonological alternation. The post does not print a single surface tone pattern for the trisyllabic string, because the cited source covers the disyllabic case only and trisyllabic output is grouping-dependent.

Tatoeba tokenisation: the raw reported count is 511 and only 31 survive inspection — a 6.1% survival rate, so any figure quoted off the raw count runs ~16× too high. 309 of the 511 contain neither 我想 nor 想你. The false positives are themselves evidence: 我很想你, 我非常想你, 我想念你 all translate with 'miss', while 我想看你 and 我想親吻你 translate with 'want'.
